migrationNotes: Spine: we start with a counter where the worth of each unit falls, then follow a shop deciding its opening hours one hour at a time, add up what the right hours earn, and learn to drop costs already paid and averages that hide the last hour.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): econ-thinking-at-the-margin-marginal-check. Its idea, that marginal means the change in the total, is taught on the last teaching screen and tested by the transfer item.
Teaching examples (cones, a florist, a concert ticket) differ from the practice examples (pizza, the café, the licence), so no teaching screen gives away a later answer.

lesson.title: The next unit

steps.headline: Deciding one unit at a time

lead.text: Take an ice-cream van where a cone costs £3. On a hot day the first cone is worth £9 to you. The second is worth £6, the third £4 and the fourth only £2, because each cone is less welcome than the one before. A choice about how many to buy is really a string of small choices, one cone at a time.

For each extra cone you ask what it adds and what it costs. What the extra cone adds is its marginal benefit, where marginal simply means one more. What it costs you is its marginal cost, which here is the £3 price. The first cone is worth £9 for £3, so buy it. The second is worth £6 for £3, and the third is worth £4 for £3, so buy both. The fourth is worth £2 for £3, and you stop.

afterFigure.text: The rule is to keep going while the next unit's benefit covers its cost, and to stop when it falls below. For the cones that means three. The rule asks about one extra unit at a time, whatever the total looks like.

diagram.alt: Four bars show what each ice-cream cone is worth to you, £9, £6, £4 and £2, with a dashed line at the £3 price. The first three bars are above the line and the fourth is below it.
diagram.caption: Keep buying while a cone is worth at least its £3 price. The fourth cone is worth £2, so you stop.

lead.text: Use the same rule at a pizza counter. Judge each slice on its own worth against its price, and stop at the first slice that falls short.

Costs often change from one unit to the next. Take a florist deciding how many late hours to stay open. Each extra hour brings in fewer customers than the one before, and each costs more because the staff are tired and paid extra. The hours bring £50, £40, £25 and £10, and they cost £20, £22, £30 and £35.

Go hour by hour. The first hour brings £50 and costs £20, so open it. The second brings £40 for £22, so open that too. The third brings £25 but costs £30, so it loses money. Stop there, because the fourth hour brings even less against a cost that keeps rising.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the florist never looks at all the hours at once. Each hour is judged against its own cost, and the first hour that falls short ends the search.

lead.text: A café is deciding how many late hours to open. Each extra hour brings in less than the one before and costs more in staff time. Decide hour by hour, as the florist did.

reveal.text: You compared each hour's own benefit with its own cost and stopped where an hour stopped paying. The best choice sits where marginal benefit meets marginal cost.

steps.headline: Adding up what the hours earn

lead.text: Once you know which hours to open, you can say how much the choice gains. An hour's net benefit is its benefit minus its cost. For the florist the first hour nets £50 − £20 = £30 and the second nets £40 − £22 = £18. The third nets £25 − £30 = −£5, a loss, which is why it stays closed.

The total net benefit of a plan is the sum of the net benefits of the hours in it. Opening two hours gives £30 + £18 = £48. Opening a third as well would give £48 − £5 = £43, which is less. The same happens with any hour that nets a loss, so the best plan includes every hour with a positive net benefit and no others.

diagram.alt: Bars for the florist's late hours. One view shows each hour's net benefit: £30, £18, minus £5 and minus £25. The other shows the total net benefit after each hour: £30, £48, £43 and £18.
diagram.caption: Use the buttons to see each hour, then the running total. The third hour nets a loss, so adding it lowers the total.

steps.headline: A bookshop can open late for up to four hours at £30 an hour. How many hours should it open, and what does it gain?

workedSteps.text: The four hours bring £80, £60, £40 and £20. Find each hour's net gain, which is its benefit minus its cost.
Open every hour whose net gain is positive: the first three.

steps.headline: The café opens its first three late hours. What total net benefit does it gain?

workedSteps.text: Hour 2: benefit £70, cost £35. Find its net benefit.

lead.text: Some costs are paid already, whatever you decide next. Suppose you bought a non-refundable £25 ticket for a concert, and on the night you feel ill. The £25 has gone either way. Stay home and you've lost it, and go and you've lost it too.

A cost like that is called a sunk cost. Because it is the same under every option, it can't tip a choice between them. The sensible comparison is between what going adds and what it costs from here on, which means an evening of music while ill against an evening in bed. The £25 appears on neither side.

afterFigure.text: The same holds for a business. A café that paid a licence last month has paid it whether or not it opens a fourth hour tonight, so the licence plays no part in tonight's decision. Only the extra hour's own benefit and cost matter, which is the rule we have been using all along.

diagram.alt: Two columns, stay home and go to the concert. Each holds the same already-paid £25 ticket, and below it the real difference: an evening in bed or an evening of music while ill.
diagram.caption: The £25 sits in both columns, so it can't decide between them.

lead.text: A café paid its licence fee last month and can't get it back. Apply the test from the last screen to the fee.
Staffing now gets dearer, so every hour costs £20 more than before. Decide again, hour by hour.

reveal.text: Dearer hours moved the stopping point from the third hour to the second. When marginal cost rises, the best amount falls.

lead.text: A tempting shortcut is to judge an hour by the average of the hours before it. The florist's first three hours bring £50, £40 and £25, which is £115 in total and an average of about £38 an hour. Set that against the third hour's £30 cost and it looks comfortably worth opening.

The average hides what the third hour itself did. The first two hours bring £90, and adding the third lifts the total from £90 to £115. So the third hour's marginal benefit is £115 − £90 = £25, which is below its £30 cost. The average was £38, yet the hour that actually decided things earned £25.

afterFigure.text: Marginal means the change in the total from one more unit, so you find it by subtracting one total from the next. Judge the extra hour by that figure and by its own cost, since the hours already open stay open either way.

diagram.alt: A bar of the florist's first three hours, £50, £40 and £25, totalling £115. The second view picks out the third hour, £25, against its £30 cost.
diagram.caption: The average of £38 hides that the third hour adds only £25. Use the buttons to move from the average to the hour itself.

lead.text: A manager notes that the café's first four hours average £63.75 of benefit, well above the £50 that the fourth costs. She says to open it. Test her reasoning on the fourth hour alone.

reveal.text: The average includes hours that are being opened anyway. Only the extra hour's own benefit and cost decide the extra hour.

lesson.orientation: Choose how much of an activity to do by comparing marginal benefit with marginal cost, and ignore sunk costs.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You are at a pizza counter, and a slice costs £4. The first slice is wonderful. The second is good but a little less so, and by the fifth you could take it or leave it. Every extra slice is worth a bit less to you than the one before, while the price on the counter stays the same.

Most real choices come in units like this: another slice, another hour of work, another batch from the oven. We seldom choose between everything and nothing. The question is usually whether to have one more.
This lesson gives you a way of settling that question. We'll weigh one more unit at a time, follow a florist and a café as they decide how late to stay open, and see why some costs should be ignored.

intro.promise: By the end you'll decide how much to do by comparing the next unit's benefit with its cost, and ignore costs already paid.

recap.keyIdea: Decide one extra unit at a time. Keep going while the next unit's benefit covers its cost, and ignore costs already paid.

blocks.text: Back at the counter, the choice of how many has become a string of small ones. You bought four slices and opened three late hours. When costs rose the café opened only two, and the fourth hour would have lost £10 even though the average looked good.

recap.nextHook: You can now say how much one more unit is worth to one buyer, and the next lesson asks how a whole street of buyers and sellers settles on a price.

questions.prompt: A café's extra opening hours have marginal benefits of £90, £70, £55, £40 and £30, and marginal costs of £30, £35, £45, £50 and £60. How many extra hours should it open?
hints: Compare benefit and cost hour by hour.
Keep adding hours while the next one brings at least as much as it costs.
Stop before the first hour whose cost exceeds its benefit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Hours one to three each bring at least their cost (£90 > £30, £70 > £35, £55 > £45); the fourth brings £40 for £50.

questions.onCorrect: 3 hours. Each of the first three brings more than it costs; later hours would bring less than they cost.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the last hour you counted with its own cost. Does it still pay?
Hours are added only while they pay. Look for the first one that does not.
The first hour is the best deal, but later hours can still be worth opening.

questions.prompt: Total net benefit of the three hours, in pounds
hints: The net benefit of an hour is its benefit minus its cost.
Work out the net benefit of each of those hours.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: £105. Add each hour's own net benefit.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the three benefits without taking the costs off.
That adds up the costs. Net benefit is benefit minus cost.

questions.prompt: The café's hours bring marginal benefits of £90, £70, £55, £40 and £30. Its marginal costs rise by £20 to £50, £55, £65, £70 and £80. How many extra hours should it now open?
hints: Use the new costs, hour by hour.
Compare each hour's benefit with its new cost, in order.
Count the hours whose benefit still covers the cost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: £90 > £50 and £70 > £55, but £55 < £65, so it opens two hours.

questions.onCorrect: 2 hours. The third hour now brings less than it costs, so the stopping point moves earlier.

misconceptions.feedback: Use the new costs for every hour. Does the third still cover its own cost?
Hours are added only while they pay. Find the first one that does not.

questions.prompt: The fourth extra hour brings £40 of benefit and costs £50. By how many pounds does opening it change the café's net benefit?
hints: Subtract the hour's cost from its benefit.
Keep the sign, since a loss is negative.
Use that hour's figures only, not the averages.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: £40 − £50 = −£10: opening it makes the café worse off.

questions.onCorrect: −£10. Only the extra hour's own benefit and cost decide it, so opening the fourth makes the café worse off.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average benefit of four hours. Only the fourth hour's own figures decide it.
Check the sign: this hour costs more than it brings.

questions.prompt: A student values successive hours of revision at 50, 40, 30, 20 and 10 points, and each hour costs her 25 points of other activities. How many hours should she revise?
hints: Every hour costs the same here.
Compare each hour's value with that cost in turn.
Count the hours worth more than the cost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50, 40 and 30 each exceed 25; the fourth hour's 20 does not.

questions.onCorrect: 3 hours. Revise while an hour is worth more than the other activities it displaces.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the last hour you counted with its cost. Is it still worth more?
Hours count only while they are worth more than they cost. Look for the first that is not.
Every hour costs the same, so later hours can still be worth it.

questions.prompt: A cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered, whatever you decide next, is called what kind of cost? One word.
hints: Think of money that has gone for good, like a non-refundable ticket.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sunk. It is the same under every option, so it should not affect the choice.

questions.onCorrect: Sunk. It is the same under every option, so it should not affect the choice.

misconceptions.feedback: Marginal means the extra unit. The word you want describes money already gone for good.

questions.prompt: A slice of pizza costs £4. The first slice is worth £12 to you, the second £9, the third £6, the fourth £5 and the fifth £3. How many slices should you buy?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Slices worth £12, £9, £6 and £5 each beat the £4 price. The fifth is worth £3, so stop.

hints: Compare each slice's worth with its price, one at a time.
Is the next slice still worth more than its price?
Stop before the first slice worth less than its price.
questions.onCorrect: 4 slices. You kept buying while the next slice was worth its price. That is thinking at the margin.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the last slice you counted: is it worth more than its price?
The first slice is the best deal, but later slices can still be worth more than their price.
Check the slice after your last one. Is it still worth more than its price?

questions.prompt: A café's first two late hours bring £160 in total; the first three bring £215. What is the marginal benefit of the third hour?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 215 − 160 = £55: the extra the third hour adds.

hints: Marginal means the change from adding one more.
questions.onCorrect: £55. Marginal means one more: the change in the total when you add the third hour.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total for three hours. The marginal figure is the change from adding the third.
That is the average per hour. The marginal figure is only what the third hour adds.

questions.prompt: Why stop after the third hour?

choices.label: The fourth hour costs more than it brings, so it lowers the total.
A shop should always stop after three hours.
Later hours are never worth opening.

acceptedIdeas: The fourth hour costs more than it brings, so it lowers the total.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The fourth hour adds £20 and costs £30, so the total would fall by £10.

hints: Compare the fourth hour's benefit with its cost.
questions.onCorrect: An hour is worth opening only while its benefit covers its cost.

misconceptions.feedback: There is no fixed number. It depends on where an hour's benefit drops below its cost.
Later hours can pay if their benefit covers their cost. This one's does not.

questions.prompt: Net benefit of hour 2, in pounds
hints: Net benefit is benefit minus cost.
Use hour 2's own benefit and cost.
Take the cost off the benefit.
questions.onCorrect: £35: benefit minus cost for that hour alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the benefit alone. Take the cost off.
That is the total for all three hours. Find hour 2 on its own.

questions.prompt: The café paid a £200 licence last month and cannot get it back. Should that £200 count when it decides whether to open a fourth hour?

choices.label: No: it is the same whichever it chooses.
Yes: the extra hour must earn it back.
Yes, but only part of it.

acceptedIdeas: No: it is the same whichever it chooses.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The licence is paid whether the café opens the extra hour or not, so it cannot change the comparison.

hints: Does the licence cost change if the café opens the extra hour?
questions.onCorrect: No. A sunk cost is the same under every option, so it cannot tip the choice.

misconceptions.feedback: The licence is paid either way, so the extra hour does not add to it.
No part of it changes with the decision, so none of it belongs in the comparison.

questions.prompt: A bakery can run up to four extra batches. The first adds £120 and each later batch adds £30 less than the one before. Every batch costs £50 to run. What total net benefit does the best number of batches give, in pounds?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first three batches each beat £50: nets of £70, £40 and £10. Total 70 + 40 + 10 = £120. The fourth adds £30 for £50, so stop.

hints: Work out which batches bring more than they cost.
Find the net benefit of each of those batches.
Add the net benefits of the batches you keep.
questions.onCorrect: £120. Keep the batches that cover their cost, then add their net benefits.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the benefits of the batches you keep without taking costs off.
Check which batches you keep. Stop at the first one that does not cover its cost.
That counts four batches' worth of net benefit. Drop any batch whose cost is higher than its benefit.
